reason: The text depicts Yahweh as directly engaged and actively involved rather than remote or emotionally removed. God engages in immediate dialogue with Moses (וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל־ מֹשֶׁה and later וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל־ מֹשֶׁה מַה־ תִּצְעַ֖ק אֵלָ֑י), demonstrating responsiveness to human concerns. God is actively involved in specific outcomes: hardening Pharaoh's heart, commanding precise actions, and executing the miraculous parting of the sea with personal intervention (וַיּ֣וֹלֶךְ יְהוָ֣ה אֶת־ הַ֠יָּם). The repeated phrase about getting glory (וְאִכָּבְדָ֤ה) shows intentional, emotionally invested goals. While the passage certainly portrays God as all-powerful, it contradicts the characterization of remoteness and emotional distance—showing instead a God dynamically engaged in the details of history and directly communicative with human actors.
